# XAML Diagnostics

Visual Studio injects a small runtime component (the "TAP") into XAML apps that are launched with the debugger.
The TAP reports the live element tree, property values, binding failures and hot reload results back to Visual Studio.
The `xaml_*` tools read and change that live state. They work only while a supported app is running.

## Start here

1. Call `xaml_get_status`. It returns everything about the session in one call: `debuggerState`, each connected app (app key `a1`, `a2`, ..., platform, capabilities, source info, and its windows with IDs, bounds and DPI), the hot reload state and errors, and `issues`.
2. If no app is listed, or something is missing, relay its `issues` (each has `evidence` and `fix`).
   For more causes and fixes, read [enablement and troubleshooting](references/enablement-and-troubleshooting.md).
3. Pick the workflow below that matches the user's goal.

## Tools

| Tool | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `xaml_get_status` | Start here, and re-check after anything goes wrong: debugger state, connected apps (platform, capabilities, source info, windows), hot reload options/state/errors, and why the Live Visual Tree, source info, or hot reload isn't working. |
| `xaml_get_visual_tree` | Read the live element tree. Page deeper with `rootElementId`. |
| `xaml_find_elements` | Find elements by type, `x:Name`, or XAML file and line. `type` and `name` accept `*` and `?` wildcards (`*Window`, `*Button`, `Save*`) and `|` alternatives (`Save|Cancel`), not regular expressions; `namedOnly=true` lists every element with an `x:Name`. |
| `xaml_get_element_properties` | Read live property values and where each value comes from. For items that aren't elements, use a path in `nameFilter`: `ColumnDefinitions[*]` lists every Grid column with its Width and ActualWidth. Get, set and explain all accept paths such as `ColumnDefinitions[2].Width`. |
| `xaml_get_element_styles` | List the styles, theme styles, triggers and templates that set properties on an element, and which setters win. |
| `xaml_explain_property_value` | Explain property values: the full precedence chain, the winner, and what to change. Explains every property on every element; `pairwise=true` pairs `elementIds[i]` with `propertyNames[i]` to check a different property per element in one call. |
| `xaml_find_resource` | Resolve a resource key the way the app does: every definition in lookup order, the winner, shadowed duplicates, file and line. |
| `xaml_get_resource_dictionaries` | List the resource dictionaries in scope (merged, theme, source URIs) and the active theme. |
| `xaml_set_element_property` | Change a property at runtime to try a fix. The change isn't saved to source. Values must be literal (`Red`, `10,0`); markup extensions such as `{Binding}` are rejected, so try those by editing XAML. Setting a bound property removes its binding on that instance. |
| `xaml_get_element_bounds` | Get screen and window coordinates, DPI scale, and visibility for elements. |
| `xaml_hit_test` | Find out whether a real click or tap reaches an element: what's on top at that point, which ancestor hides or disables it, its effective opacity, and how much ancestors clip it. |
| `xaml_explain_visibility` | Answer "why can't I see this element" in one call: hidden or transparent ancestors, zero size and why (Grid row/column, explicit size), empty text, foreground matching the background, clipping, covering elements, and binding failures that target it. |
| `xaml_audit_styles` | Check that every control of a type looks the same: which style each instance uses, the values of key properties, the outliers, and hard-coded values in XAML that override the style. |
| `xaml_interact` | Click, toggle, select, expand, type into, focus, scroll to, or hover over an element through UI Automation. Pass `checkProperties` (and `checkElementIds` for effects elsewhere) to get before/after values and `changed`, so a click that does nothing is caught in the same call. |
| `xaml_select_element` | Select an element in the Live Visual Tree and open its XAML source. |
| `xaml_capture_image` | See the app (window IDs come from `xaml_get_status`). Use this to verify every visual change. |
| `xaml_get_binding_failures` / `xaml_clear_binding_failures` | Read the binding failures log (with XAML file and line), or clear it before a retest. |
| `xaml_run_accessibility_check` / `xaml_get_accessibility_results` | Find accessibility issues (WPF and WinUI desktop). |
| `xaml_get_hot_reload_log` | Read recent XAML and .NET hot reload log output (`xaml_get_status` has the options, state and errors). |
| `xaml_apply_hot_reload` | Push saved XAML edits (and, optionally, code edits) into the running app. |

Tools that take `elementIds` (properties, styles, explain, set, hit test, bounds) accept a list. Pass every element you need in one call instead of calling once per element; `xaml_explain_property_value` also takes several `propertyNames`, and `xaml_set_element_property` takes several `setters` (`"Name=Value"`) and `resetProperties`. With one item you get that item's result; with several you get `results[]`, where an item that failed has its own `error` and the others still succeed.

Element IDs look like `a1:123456`. They're valid only while the element exists.
Hot reload, template changes, and switching tabs or pages recreate elements. A named element can be addressed as `#Name` (its `x:Name`, for example `#SaveButton`) anywhere an element ID is accepted; names keep working across hot reloads, so prefer them for elements you'll check again after a fix. Numeric IDs of named elements are re-resolved automatically when they go stale.
If a tool returns `ELEMENT_GONE`, query the tree again.
Every error result has `error`, `message`, and usually a `hint`. Follow the hint before trying anything else.
Results are kept under about 16 KB. When a list is cut, the result says which list and how many entries were omitted (`omittedNote`); narrow the request rather than repeating it.

To read the view model behind an element, pass `nameFilter="DataContext.IsBusy|ErrorMessage"` (or `DataContext.Order.Total`; MAUI uses `BindingContext.`) to `xaml_get_element_properties`. This is usually faster and safer than pausing the debugger to evaluate expressions. Element properties and view-model members can be read in one call: `nameFilter="Text|IsEnabled|DataContext.IsBusy"`.

## Workflows

### Fix binding failures
The binding failures list is a cumulative log, not live state. An entry stays listed after its cause is fixed, and a binding only fails (and is logged) once the UI that uses it has been shown. A view created after a hot reload (a reopened dialog, a new tab) first loads the compiled XAML from the last build and then gets your edits, so it can log the old binding's failures once even though it ends up showing the right data. Check the bound values on that view (`xaml_get_element_properties` or a capture) before reporting such a failure as still present; the next build and restart removes it.

1. Call `xaml_get_binding_failures`. Each entry has the binding path, the target element and property, the data context type, the description, and the XAML file and line.
   Entries with a XAML file come first and are the ones to fix. Entries without a file usually come from bindings created in code; they matter less.
2. Open the XAML file and the data context type (the view model). Fix the path, the `DataContext`, the `Source`/`ElementName`/`RelativeSource`, the converter, or the missing property in the view model.
3. Look for failures that haven't been logged yet. Views that were never shown (other tabs, popups, dialogs, items that weren't loaded) haven't run their bindings.
   - Check their XAML statically against the view models, with the same checks as step 2.
   - To catch the rest at runtime, call `xaml_clear_binding_failures`, then show each view: select each tab, open each popup and dialog, and expand each section. Use `xaml_interact`, or ask the user. Then call `xaml_get_binding_failures`.
4. Apply the fixes. See [Apply a fix to the running app](#apply-a-fix-to-the-running-app).
5. Verify: call `xaml_clear_binding_failures`, show every view you changed again, then call `xaml_get_binding_failures`.
   Hot reload only updates elements in the live tree, so a view that wasn't loaded is updated when it's next shown. It can briefly log its old failures as it loads. If a failure comes back once, show the view again before deciding the fix didn't work.
   Without clearing, read `occurrencesSinceLastRead` (0 means it hasn't failed again since your previous read) and `pathStillInSource` (false means the XAML no longer has that path, so the entry is a leftover from before your fix).

### Apply a fix to the running app
Don't build the app while it's being debugged. The running app locks its build output, so the build fails or its result isn't loaded.

- **XAML-only edits:** save the files, then call `xaml_apply_hot_reload`. Read `summary` first, then `errors` (this call), `codeHotReloadWarnings` (a code change that needs a restart; tell the user) and `earlierErrors` (an earlier update; may already be fixed). If something looks wrong, call `xaml_get_status` and read `hotReload`. `alreadyApplied` means hot reload pushed changes within the last minute, usually your edit as you made it. For `noChange`, compare times: if `lastHotReloadUpdate.secondsAgo` is after your edit, it reached the app; if it's null or older, it didn't.
  Hot reload doesn't wire up a new event attribute (`Click="OnSubscribe"`) on an existing element, even after the handler is added with .NET Hot Reload; the element keeps its old handlers until it's recreated. During a live session, prefer a `Command` binding or a trigger, or say the handler needs a restart and don't report it as verified. Values that code already set (constructors, `Loaded` handlers) also stay until that code runs again.
- **Code edits (code-behind, view models, converters):** save the files, then call `xaml_apply_hot_reload` with `includeCodeChanges=true`. This starts .NET Hot Reload, like the Hot Reload toolbar button. Read `codeHotReloadOutput` in the result.
  Keep code edits additive while the app runs: add or change method bodies and properties, but don't delete or rename types, members or fields, and don't change signatures. Leave now-unused code in place and mention it so the user can clean it up after the session.
  `x:Name` fields keep the element type the app was built with. If you change an element's type in XAML (for example a Border to a ToggleButton), code-behind can't use the new type's members until a rebuild. Wire the new element with a binding or command in XAML instead.
  Read `codeStatus` in the result: `failed` means the running app still has the old code, even if the XAML part applied (`applied` is then false; `xamlApplied` reports the XAML part).
  An edit that can't be hot reloaded makes Visual Studio show a "Hot Reload - Changes not supported" prompt (`visualStudioPromptOpen=true`). Tell the user, and don't call more tools until they choose.
- To check that code compiles without stopping the debug session, rely on the editor's errors. Don't run `dotnet build` or MSBuild on the project being debugged.
- After a fix is applied, call `xaml_capture_image` to see the result.

### Find out why something looks wrong
1. Find the element. Prefer `xaml_find_elements` (by `x:Name`, type, or XAML file and line) over reading the whole tree. To see a part of the tree, call `xaml_get_visual_tree` with that element as `rootElementId`.
2. Use `xaml_capture_image` to see it.
3. Use `xaml_get_element_properties` to see each value's source. A local value overrides a style, a style overrides an inherited value, and so on. Look at parent elements too: layout depends on them.
4. Optionally, try a fix with `xaml_set_element_property`, then capture again.
   To compare design options, apply each variant with `xaml_set_element_property`, capture it, then set the original values back before the next one. If the user said they'll pick one, show the captures and stop; edit the source only after they choose.
5. Make the permanent fix in the XAML source, save, call `xaml_apply_hot_reload`, and capture again to confirm.
6. For blurry or soft rendering, compare live geometry with what the source implies:
   - Fractional `screen` pixel positions from `xaml_get_element_bounds` (for example x=18.75) put 1-px lines across two pixels. Look for fractional margins or padding up the parent chain and whether `UseLayoutRounding` is set (WPF).
   - An `Image` whose rendered size differs from its bitmap's pixel size is resampled. Prefer the native size (`Stretch="None"` or matching Width/Height) or a vector icon over changing the scaling mode.
   - An `Effect` (such as `DropShadowEffect`) on an element that contains text renders that text as a bitmap. Move the effect to a sibling behind the content.
   - A `Viewbox` or scale transform renders content at a non-1 scale; compare the element's rendered bounds with its declared size.

### A control can't be clicked, or can't be seen
1. Find the control (an app's own subclasses need wildcards: `type="*Button"`, `type="*Window"`).
   If it can't be seen at all, call `xaml_explain_visibility` first: it walks the element and its ancestors and returns ranked `causes`, each with the element, property, value source and XAML location to fix.
   A hidden element often has several stacked causes. Causes with `latent=true` are masked by another cause today (a collapsed button can't be measured or hit-tested) but will keep it hidden after that one is fixed. Report and fix every cause, not only the first.
   When the user says something is missing ("where is my Save button?", "I can't see X"), they want it back: fix every cause, apply the fix, then call `xaml_explain_visibility` again until it finds none and confirm with `xaml_capture_image`. Only stop at an explanation when the user asked just for one.
2. Call `xaml_hit_test` with its `elementIds` (and `points` to test spots other than the center). Read `summary` first.
   - `inputTarget` that isn't the element or its descendant means something is on top. The `stack` lists everything under the point, topmost first, with its XAML location. Typical causes: a transparent overlay or adorner with a non-null `Background`, a later sibling in the same `Grid` cell, or a negative margin.
   - `blockers` name the ancestor that sets `Visibility`, `IsHitTestVisible=False`, `IsEnabled=False`, or `Opacity=0`. `IsEnabledCore` means the command's `CanExecute` returned false; look at the view model, not the XAML.
   - `visibleFraction` below 1 and `clippedBy` show the ancestor (a `ScrollViewer`, a fixed-size `Grid` row or column, `ClipToBounds`) that cuts it off.
3. `xaml_interact invoke` uses UI Automation and bypasses hit testing, so it can succeed when a real click wouldn't. Don't treat a successful `invoke` as proof the user can click it; use `xaml_hit_test`.
4. Fix the source (for example `IsHitTestVisible="False"` or `Background="{x:Null}"` on the overlay), hot reload, then call `xaml_hit_test` again. WinUI and UWP use the platform's own hit testing; MAUI approximates it from bounds, `IsVisible`, `InputTransparent` and `IsEnabled`, so confirm a MAUI result with `xaml_get_element_bounds` and the visual tree order. If `supportsHitTest` is false for the app (an older TAP), use those instead.

### A style, setter, or resource isn't applying
1. Find the element, then call `xaml_explain_property_value` for the wrong property. The chain shows which source wins. For example, a local value beats any style setter, and a style trigger beats a style setter. When the value is a Binding, DynamicResource or other markup extension, `evaluatedValue` is what the app actually uses now (WPF). `evaluatedValue=null` on a DynamicResource means the key didn't resolve.
2. Call `xaml_get_element_styles` to see which styles apply at all. If the expected style is missing, check its `x:Key`, `TargetType` and `BasedOn`. Common WPF reasons an implicit (unkeyed) style doesn't reach an element:
   - **Subclass:** implicit styles need the exact type. A `MyButton : Button` needs its own implicit style `BasedOn` the Button style.
   - **Container style keys:** `ToolBar` applies `ToolBar.ButtonStyleKey` (and similar keys for other controls) to its buttons instead of the implicit style.
   - **Closer implicit style:** an implicit style in a nearer `Resources` (a panel or the Window) replaces the outer one completely unless it's `BasedOn` it.
   - **Template boundary:** inside a `DataTemplate` or `ControlTemplate`, implicit styles for elements that aren't `Control`s (TextBlock, Border...) come only from the template's own resources, `App.xaml`, or the theme; Window- or panel-level ones don't apply. Compare a TextBlock inside an ItemsControl's template with one outside it.
   - **Resource shadowing:** a dictionary merged later redefines a key the style uses.

   When the user asks about "every element", check every kind of element the style dictionary or page styles target (text, borders, and items in templates, not only buttons), and look at items generated from templates. `xaml_audit_styles` with `type` (for example `*Button`) does this in one call: it groups the instances by the style they use, lists outliers, and lists hard-coded XAML values that override the style. Pass `expected` (`"Background=#FF0078D4|FontSize=14"`) when the design values are known.
3. Call `xaml_find_resource` with the key and the `elementId`, so the element's and ancestors' resources are searched too. `found=false` means the dictionary isn't in scope: it isn't merged into `App.xaml` or an ancestor, or the key is misspelled. Several definitions mean one shadows another; the `effective` one wins.
4. Call `xaml_get_resource_dictionaries` to confirm which dictionaries are loaded and merged, and which theme dictionary is active (`ThemeResource` on WinUI and UWP).
5. Fix the XAML, hot reload, and check again with `xaml_explain_property_value` and `xaml_capture_image`.
6. If the fix is in a resource dictionary that app code loads at runtime (for example a theme file added to `MergedDictionaries` by a theme switcher), hot reload may not update the instance the app already loaded, even though the apply reports success. Verify with `xaml_find_resource`. If it still shows the old value, trigger the code path again (for example switch the theme away and back with `xaml_interact`) before concluding; only then tell the user a restart is needed to see that change.

### Items use the wrong DataTemplate
1. Look under the ItemsControl's containers (`ContentPresenter`, `ListBoxItem`...) in `xaml_get_visual_tree`: the generated children show which template each item actually got. `xaml_get_element_properties` on the presenter gives the item's runtime type in `Content`.
2. `ContentTemplate` is usually empty because implicit lookup picks the template; that's normal. Call `xaml_get_resource_dictionaries` (with the list's `elementId` and keys) to see which DataTemplate keys are in scope for the list.
3. WPF implicit DataTemplate lookup by `DataType` only matches when: the template has no `x:Key`; `DataType` is the exact runtime class (same namespace and assembly, not an interface; a base class matches only if no closer template exists); and the template is in the item's resource scope (the list, its ancestors, Window or App resources, not a sibling panel). A `DataTemplateSelector` or `ItemTemplate` on the list overrides all of this.
4. Fix, hot reload, then capture and check each item kind.

### Fix accessibility issues
1. Call `xaml_run_accessibility_check`. Each issue has the rule, description, how to fix it, the element (name, class, AutomationId), and the XAML location when known. The results also appear in the Accessibility Checker pane. If it returns `CANCELED`, the user pressed Stop: don't rerun it on your own, ask first.
2. Fix the source. Typical fixes: `AutomationProperties.Name` or `LabeledBy`, a missing `x:Uid`/`Name` on interactive controls, contrast, focusability, and keyboard access. When a visible label already describes a control (a "Search" TextBlock next to a TextBox), prefer `AutomationProperties.LabeledBy="{Binding ElementName=...}"` over a duplicated hard-coded name.
3. Hot reload, then run the check again.
4. A clean scan is **not** a full audit. The checker runs the automated Axe.Windows UI Automation rules only. It does not check text contrast, and it can't see problems in elements that aren't in the UIA control tree. When the user asks to fix "every" issue, also review these with the other tools before you report the app clean:
   - **Mouse-only interaction**: elements with click handlers (`MouseLeftButtonUp`, `Tapped`, `PointerPressed`, `Cursor="Hand"`) that aren't controls. They aren't focusable or keyboard-reachable and have no role. Replace them with a `Button` (restyled if needed) rather than adding `Focusable`.
   - **Images and icons**: give informative images (cover art, avatars, status icons) an `AutomationProperties.Name`. Mark purely decorative ones so screen readers skip them (WinUI/UWP: `AutomationProperties.AccessibilityView="Raw"`).
   - **Text contrast**: for text with a light or custom `Foreground`, call `xaml_explain_property_value` on `Foreground` and the effective background and check WCAG AA (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text). Light grays such as `#BBB`–`#CCC` on white fail.
   - **List and grid items**: an item whose data template has no name gets its automation name from the item's `ToString()` (often the type name, for example `MyApp.Episode`). Bind `AutomationProperties.Name` in the `ItemContainerStyle` (or override `ToString`).
   - **Text inputs and sliders** with no visible label association.

### Hot reload didn't apply
1. Call `xaml_get_status` and read `hotReload` for options, state, and current errors (with file and line).
2. Call `xaml_get_hot_reload_log` with `errorsOnly=true` for recent messages.
3. Explain the cause. Common causes: the file wasn't saved, a platform is disabled, a XAML parse error, or an unsupported edit such as `x:Class`, new event handlers, or new types that need a rebuild. See [enablement and troubleshooting](references/enablement-and-troubleshooting.md#hot-reload).

### The Live Visual Tree is empty or has no source info
Call `xaml_get_status` and read `issues`. The usual fixes are: launch with F5 instead of attaching, use a Debug build, enable the platform in options, and for attach scenarios set `ENABLE_XAML_DIAGNOSTICS_SOURCE_INFO=1` before the app starts.

### Slow lists, scrolling or startup
Measure, don't guess. Lists are slow when UI virtualization is off and a container is created for every item.
1. Count realized containers: `xaml_find_elements` with `type="ListBoxItem"` (or `ListViewItem`, `DataGridRow`, `TreeViewItem`). `totalMatches` near the item count means virtualization is off; a virtualized list realizes only about a screenful.
2. `xaml_get_element_bounds` on the list: a height far beyond the window means it's measured with infinite height (inside a `ScrollViewer` or a vertical `StackPanel`).
3. Check the ancestors in the result's `path`, and the list's properties: `ScrollViewer.CanContentScroll="False"`, grouping without `VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping="True"`, a non-virtualizing `ItemsPanel`, and `VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizing="False"` each turn virtualization off on their own.
4. When the user wants to see the effect of each change, make **one change at a time**: edit, hot reload, then count and capture again. Several blockers stack, so the count may only drop after the last one is fixed. Say so rather than skipping the per-change measurements.
5. Hot reload can't re-run startup, so startup time in the running app stays stale. To measure it, restart the debug session (stop debugging and press F5, or ask the user to). Don't build a separate copy into another folder or launch extra instances of the app.

### Reproduce a problem by driving the UI
1. Find the control with `xaml_find_elements` (for example `type="Button"`, `name="SaveButton"`).
2. Call `xaml_interact` with `invoke`, `toggle`, `select`, `expand`, or `setValue`. To switch tabs or pick a list item, `select` the `TabItem`, `ListBoxItem`, or `ComboBoxItem` itself.
   If the element doesn't support the action, the error lists its supported patterns: try the containing control instead (for example the `Button` instead of its `TextBlock`).
   If the result says the action hasn't finished, an app event handler is still running (often a modal dialog). Don't repeat the action; capture an image to see what's showing.
   `setValue` replaces the text as if the user typed it, but focus stays put. A WPF `TextBox.Text` binding with the default `LostFocus` trigger doesn't update its source until focus moves; the result says so. Use `focus` on another control to mimic tabbing away. If the bug report says something only updates "after I click somewhere else", that difference is the clue.
3. Check the effect with `xaml_capture_image`, `xaml_get_element_properties`, or `xaml_get_binding_failures`.
4. Use `xaml_get_element_bounds` to reason about layout: overlap, clipping, off-screen, or zero-size elements. `isVisible` only reflects `Visibility`; `clippedByWindow` and `insideWindowFraction` tell you whether the user can actually see it. `xaml_hit_test` adds ancestor clipping, effective opacity, and what's on top.
5. For mouse-only states such as `IsMouseOver` (hover styles, tooltips, hover-revealed buttons), call `xaml_interact` with `action="hover"` (optionally `value="x,y"` in DIPs inside the element), then capture or read properties; call `action="unhover"` when done. Hover moves the user's real mouse pointer over the app window, so mention it, and it fails if another window covers the spot. `IsPressed` and drag states still can't be driven: prove them from the precedence chain instead. `xaml_explain_property_value` shows which layer wins now, and whether a higher layer such as a local value or an animation would beat a trigger. Inactive triggers aren't reported, so read the `Triggers` in the style's source (its `location` in `xaml_get_element_styles`).
6. To verify a view-model or code-behind fix, re-run the code path through the UI (`xaml_interact` on the button or command that triggers it) and read the bound values with `xaml_get_element_properties`. A C# hot reload fix only affects code that runs after it's applied. If the code only runs once (a constructor or a Loaded handler), say that the running app still has the old state and that a restart is the real check. Only evaluate it in the debugger if the user wants live proof.
7. To test other window sizes, set the Window element's `Width`/`Height` with `xaml_set_element_property`. These are DIPs, while window `bounds` from `xaml_get_status` are physical pixels (`Width = bounds.width / dpiScale`). When the user says "800 px", state which unit you tested, or test both. Put the window back to its original size and `WindowState` before you finish, and check with `xaml_get_status` that it isn't minimized or off-screen.

**Don't pause the debugger while using these tools.** In break mode the app's UI thread is frozen, so `xaml_*` calls fail with `DEBUGGER_PAUSED`, hot reload applies nothing, and tree results come from a stale cache. `xaml_get_status` reports `debuggerState`. **Check it first.** If it's `paused` (because the user, you, a sub-agent, a breakpoint or an exception broke in), call `debugger_continue` before anything else (or ask the user to press Continue/F5 if they said they paused on purpose), then retry. Don't edit and "verify" while paused. If an exception broke in, read it with the debugger tools first, because it may be the bug. Remove any breakpoints you set so the app doesn't break again. Debugger expression evaluation can show the user an "Allow" prompt for side effects, even in Autopilot.

If these tools return `UNSUPPORTED_BY_TAP` (for example, an older runtime component under the remote debugger), use the debugger's `debugger_ui_tree`, `debugger_ui_interact`, and `debugger_screenshot` tools with the element's `AutomationProperties.AutomationId` or `Name`.

## Rules

- Runtime changes made with `xaml_set_element_property` are lost when the app restarts. Always make the real fix in the source files.
- Keep the app's intended design. A local value that deliberately differs from the style (for example one control with its own accent color, or a code comment that says how it should look) should survive the fix; make the style apply underneath it instead of deleting it. Never edit comments or docs to match your change.
- `xaml_interact` acts on the user's running app as if they clicked or typed. Don't invoke destructive commands (delete, send, purchase, close) unless the user asked for it.
- Prefer to edit the source, then call `xaml_apply_hot_reload` and `xaml_capture_image` to verify. Don't build the app while it's being debugged, and don't ask the user to restart unless hot reload can't apply the change.
- Property values and screenshots can contain user data. Use them only to diagnose the user's problem.
- When writing or changing XAML, follow [XAML authoring guidance](references/xaml-authoring.md) so the XAML works well with hot reload, the XAML designer, and diagnostics. It lists the mistakes that most often cause binding failures, unclickable or invisible controls, slow lists, and styles that don't apply. Check new XAML against it before saving.
